speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have made inquiries and find that the Times-Gazette, published in Oshawa, reported that the federation of printing

Inquiries of the Ministry trades unions had passed a resolution demanding that the federal government accord to the civil servants the right to belong to a union of their choice and to bargain collectively.
I have no knowledge of any regulation or order of any kind which prevents any civil servant from joining the union of his choice.
The matter of collective bargaining raises a question of principle. Employees of the public service are recruited by the civil service commission, through competitive examinations advertised across the country, and a choice is made on the basis of merit, irrespective of union affiliations. The same principle of technical qualification is applied in connection with promotions, and there is no discrimination between employees, whether they belong to unions or not.
It is not considered that it would be in the interests of the service to exclude non-union citizens from free access to government employment.

Mr. Speaker, I listened to the debate on this
bill, and to that on another bill amending the Excise Tax Act. There will be a third bill concerning the income tax.
I noticed that during the debate some members said that there are some good features in the bill. This puzzled me, because taxation is always unpleasant. I cannot see why or how anyone could rejoice about new taxes. On the other hand, I admire once again the wisdom of the government. I did not favour the $65 million gift to the western farmers, but as I listened to numerous requests for a gift amounting to nearly five times more, I wondered what other good features those hon. members who are satisfied with taxation would have suggested to the government in order to pay for that surplus gift.
They like taxation; they want more gifts. How would they pay for them? This has puzzled me greatly. I now speak as the man in' the street who has read in the press numerous requests for more gifts, and who is puzzled to see that those who make the requests complain about taxation. Besides that, those who continuously ask for more money for defence cannot complain about taxation, especially taxation of this kind. They agree that they want more expenditures, yet they combat taxation and offer no substitute or alternative. If the government had considered favourably the numerous requests for more gifts to the western farmers, and more expenditures for national defence, I wonder what the suggestion of those hon. members would have been, in the way of new taxation.
It is easy to complain about taxation. But one of the foremost principles of democracy is the rule of the majority. Minorities may express their dissent or disagreement, but after a decision is reached by the majority we must stand by that decision, especially if the majority is composed of gentlemen who agree as to the necessity for an expenditure.
To summarize what I have said, I do not consider that there are any good features in the three bills, the one before the house at this time and the two others, but I consider that they are necessary. As the expenditures have been agreed to, the taxpayer must foot the bill. I realize that if any other party or group had been in power, things would have been much worse than they are now.

The house resumed, from Monday, June 4, consideration in committee of Bill No. 294, to amend the Excise Tax Act-Mr. Abbott-Mr. Dion in the chair.
On section 2-Duty paid value.

When the
committee rose last night we were considering section 2. As I understand it, the parliamentary assistant had asked us to accept this section, partly on the ground that it agreed with the wording of section 5, which I understood him to say was of long standing and contained a wording which had been worked on and therefore we should accept it. I note that the explanatory note opposite section 5 reads:
The purpose of this amendment is to provide clearer definitions of "duty paid value" and "sale price," for purposes of part XIII of the act under which the consumption or sales tax is imposed.
Therefore I do not think the parliamentary assistant can ask us to accept the wording of section 2 as being sacrosanct merely because it is the same as section 5. That reminds me of a situation which existed years ago in Kingston. A gun was fired at twelve o'clock every day at the fort. Someone was out at the fort and asked how they got the time for the gun, and was told that they got it electrically from a jeweler in Kingston. Next day he happened to be in the jewelry store at twelve o'clock and heard the gun fired. At that moment the jeweler said, "We must set our clock; there goes the gun."
I suggest that the parliamentary assistant
IMr. Pouliot.]
is not helping us by this reference to section 5, and perhaps he might explain it further.
While I am on my feet I should like to refer to an answer which was made to a question asked by the 'hon. member for Hamilton West, and I quote from page 3715 of Hansard where the hon. member is quoted as follows:
Then if a manufacturer allows a discount for cash do you permit him to apply the sales tax to the net amount after the discount has been deducted?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
That is quite right.
Is the parliamentary assistant sure of that?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
When this question was raised last night I was perhaps not as well briefed as I should, be, mainly because we were then dealing with the existing act whereas I had got prepared on the details of the amending bill. It is generally in connection with the changes that the department and I do our homework. First of all let me say that the details of section 79 (b) (ii) ar.e not the result of circumstances similar to those affecting the jeweler in Kingston. The question goes back to the time of Right Hon. R. B. Bennett, who was minister of finance as well as prime minister in 1934. In order to avoid the full effect of the sales tax, certain manufacturers, notably automobile manufacturers, sought to break up what was regarded as their sale price into items such as manufacture, advertising, servicing. The dealer or the retailer paid the full price, but then it was claimed by the manufacturers that the sales tax applied only to the cost of the manufacture of the car. It was because of that that this section was first spelled out so far as sales tax is concerned. Then I have found that in the schedule of the present act it is spelled out with respect to automobiles so far as the excise tax is concerned.
Let me go through each of these items and give examples. First of all there is advertising. Every national manufacturer advertises his product nationally, whether it be a car, a radio or a television set. Undoubtedly that is reflected in the actual sale price to the wholesaler or jobber of that item. I am informed that some manufacturers, such as radio manufacturers, actually specify it as being two and one-half per cent of the selling price of their goods to the wholesaler or jobber to whom they sell.
The next one is financing. This brings in the matter of cash discounts, referred to by the hon. member for Hamilton West. If the manufacturer in selling his product to the jobber or wholesaler has to finance that sale, that again is a cost to him of selling the article, a cost which is properly included in his selling price. If the buyer, however,

finances it through a finance company, that is different; it is not a cost to the manufacturer. If the manufacturer, as suggested last night by the hon. member for Hamilton West, has to turn to a finance company to finance it, then that is an operation of the manufacturer which is reflected in the selling price. So far as cash discount is concerned, I must confess that after giving that answer last night I thought it over and wondered how allowance would be made for a cash discount, since most manufacturers of course sell with the thought that purchases will be paid for in thirty, sixty or ninety days.
The customs and excise branch of the Department of National Revenue does not demand payment for sales and excise taxes collected in this month until the end of the next month. Therefore purchases made at the first of the month have sixty days to run, and those at the end of the month have thirty days to run, the average being forty-five days. Most cash sales are for ten days. You pay in ten days, or at the outside thirty days, and you get the benefit of the cash discount. Therefore the manufacturer still has in his possession the invoice of sale, and if there has been a cash discount he takes that off his selling price and the sales tax is levied on the remainder. That is an accepted practice of the trade.
The next matter is servicing.

Before the parliamentary
assistant leaves that point, I do not wish to contradict him, but 1 can tell him that the practice of the trade is not as he says. Manufacturers always charge sales tax on the invoice price. Then if you take your cash discount afterward you save that amount; but certainly at no time do you get a rebate on the sales or excise tax that has been paid.

I am again informed-and I
went over this point very carefully with the officials of the department-that credit is given in the cash discount for the amount of sales tax which might have been paid on the total price, including servicing.

If the individual can get a discount, the manufacturer shows it on the invoice and pays his sales tax on the net selling price to the jobber or wholesaler, or, if he should sell directly, to the retailer.
The next point was servicing, and the difference between servicing and a warranty. Taking again the example of an automobile, because it is the easiest one to use, the warranty is that for the first six months or first year they will not only service the article but will replace defective parts, and, if need be, replace the whole article if it should prove to be defective. That is a warranty. Aside from that there are, as all hon. members know, servicing guarantees given on cars and other such items. An automobile manufacturer will service your car for the first
10.000	miles. It may take some people a year, some two years, and some even three years to use up the 10,000 mile service guarantee given by the automobile manufacturer, which servicing is still one of the costs included in the selling price of the manufacturer to the dealer.

manufacturers who give 10,000 mile service. I think it is 4,000 miles or ninety days, whichever comes first.

The actual details are a

The last matter is commission. Some manufacturers sell their goods through their own salesmen who are on salary, some throug salesmen on commission, and some through salesmen on a joint salary and commission basis. It has been argued that where manufacturers pay outright commission it is not a cost of manufacture. There is no doubt that it is a cost to the man who buys the car,

Excise Tax Act
because the manufacturer's cost and the commission have been added before the person purchases the car. Again so far as the interpretation of sales price in the present act is concerned, and in the schedule so far as excise tax on cars is concerned, that has been interpreted as a part of the selling price.
I think I have answered the points the hon. member raised. '

How could commission, which presumably is paid to an intermediary, come into the manufacturer's cost?

Because the manufacturer himself has salesmen. The manufacturer does not merely sell by catalogue. It may not be so in the automobile industry, but in other industries many manufacturers have their own salesmen who go to jobbers, wholesalers, department stores and chain stores to push their products. In the actual net cost to the purchaser of those goods there is induded the cost of manufacture and these other things, plus the commission paid the salesmen of the manufacturer who in the end might sell to a jobber, wholesaler, or department store, or, in the case of direct sale, to a retailer.

I should like to get some clarification of a ruling concerning the importation of certain diamonds, in connection with which I have had several communications. This is a case in which diamonds were sent out of the country for reconditioning, I think to Antwerp. When such diamonds are sent there they are checked by the customs at that port and certified as to identification. Then the necessary repairs are, made, which I presume is simply a matter of cutting down the diamond. You cannot make a diamond larger; it has to be made smaller. This work is done and the diamond is returned through the customs at Antwerp, where it is again checked for identity. But when it comes to the Canadian side an excise tax is charged just as though it were a new stone. The original stone paid an excise tax when it was admitted to the country in the first place, and these people are greatly concerned. They say they cannot have that work done with advantage to themselves in this country, and it is therefore necessary to return such stones to the point of origin in a foreign country. When it comes back, however, they find the same tax collected as though it were a new stone, and they say they cannot charge their customers enough to carry on this sort of work economically. .
After these people wrote to the department they were informed that the ruling that the second charge was correct was based upon the fact that these stones are not easily identifiable. In the letter to which I am

referring at the moment the writer says "identical" but I think he must mean identifiable. I would like some comment on that. Does not the parliamentary assistant think that tax is unjust under those circumstances? It is an easy way out to say, "Well, how can we tell it is the same stone? Let us collect the second tax," but I think this should be looked into, and if the regulation is not justified by the facts it should be changed.
One of the letters I have had from the retail merchants' association, backing up this claim, asks that the case be reconsidered. They suggest that the ruling in this instance be clarified, since this firm definitely cannot continue to pay the customs duty on diamonds which are forwarded for reconditioning. As I say, there is no place in this country where the work can be done. This looks to me like an unjust tax, like an easy way out. If there is a process of identification, as I submit there is, then the diamonds should be identified and the tax paid only once. If the stone has been improved1 in value I suppose there could be a tax on the improvement, but I do not think it has. It has been made smaller, and has decreased in value.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
This, of course, would be primarily matter of customs administration that would come under the Customs Act which was under consideration last week. So far as I know, the only reconditioning that could be done to diamonds, to use that word loosely, would be regrinding to make a diamond smaller and with different facets. No one would have that done unless it was going to improve the value of the diamond. One would not deliberately take a diamond and have it cut down to reduce its value.
The other point is that if a manufacturing process is involved in connection with any article, whether that article be raw or semifinished, and the article is brought back into the country, naturally its value has been increased, so there are sales and excise taxes, in the case of luxury goods, on the processing which has changed that article from a semi-finished nature to a finished nature.
However, getting back to my first point, this is primarily a matter for the administration of the Department of National Revenue, so it does not quite come within the Excise Tax Act. I am quite sure, however, that the Minister of National Revenue will take note of the hon member's plea in this regard and give him an answer.

If there were an increase in
value, as the parliamentary assistant suggested, I could see the justice of charging a tax on that increased value, but not on the total value of the stone. I do not think his
Excise Tax Act
argument is well founded when he says the value has been increased, because I am comparing two values. I am comparing the value of the stone upon which the excise tax was originally paid with the value of the stone on the second occasion. A stone would be sent out to be reconditioned because it had deteriorated or been damaged so it was not worth the original cost. The comparison I am making is between the value of the diamond in the first instance, which was certainly higher, and the value in the second case; but it was upon that original value that these people had to pay their excise tax. Now, after the diamond has deteriorated and they have gone to the expense of having it made of some value, you are taxing them on the full value of the stone, which you have done already on the greater value in the first place. I do not think the first argument advanced by the parliamentary assistant holds water. I cannot see it. He gives the assurance that the Minister of National Revenue will look into the matter. Of course we have had that assurance at least once before. The matter was looked into, and I was taking this opportunity to suggest that the decision in that case was wrong. However, again I ask that the matter be looked into.

Can the parliamentary
assistant tell me the mechanics of the change in the application of the sales tax to logging truck tires? There has been a change recently, and I would like the parliamentary assistant to explain it to me.

Excise Tax Act
On section 6-Consumption or sales tax of ten per cent.

This clause, while it is brief, certainly outdoes any other provision in this bill in sheer iniquity at a time like this. This subject of the increase in the sales tax has been discussed on several occasions and I do not pretend that at this stage anything new is likely to be offered in opposition to it; nevertheless, Mr. Chairman, I do not feel disposed to let this occasion pass without again offering the strongest possible objection to this increase in the sales tax.
The minister has not made out a case for a sufficient increase in general taxation to cover the amount of money that he estimates he will derive from this increase in the sales tax; nor has he, apart from that first point, made any case for raising money by this iniquitous method.
Now, sir, we have already had no little discussion about the minister's budgeting in general; but surely, Mr. Chairman, what the minister had to say in pleading for increases in taxes to meet estimated increases in expenditure, and to balance his budget, and provide a surplus of $30 million, has been swept aside by the revenue and expenditure figures that have been disclosed for the first month of this present fiscal year. When we see, as we have seen, that the minister has a surplus for the month of April of $121,500,000, which is something vastly greater than the surplus for the month of April, 1950, the minister has no shred of excuse for seeking this increase in the sales tax.
The minister cannot deny that this is the most inflationary of all his budget proposals.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: He certainly does deny it.

Then I wish the minister would give some reasons for his assertion, because there is nothing but his plain ungarnished assertion to back up the point that he is seeking to make.
This increase in the sales tax is going to go on snowballing as the things to which it applies pass from hand to hand, from the manufacturer or producer to the wholesaler, to the jobber, to the retailer, to the consumer; and it is not going to produce an amount of revenue commensurate with what it is going to cost the consumer. Figures have already been put on Hansard-I think I know them off by heart now-which establish conclusively that even in the simplest cases this tax costs the consumer just about twice what it yields to the government in revenue. You can find other cases in which the goods are passing through more than the hands of the producer, the wholesaler, the

retailer and consumer, and also with respect to particular classes of goods, the amount that the tax in that snowballing or pyramiding process costs the consumer in mark-ups is far in excess of the amount that the government receives by way of revenue. In some of these cases it is more than double the amount of the tax. The government does not receive any more tax, but the consumer is going to be paying in these cases just about double what the government is going to collect out of it in taxes. The remainder goes to inflate the cost of living, and it will take more than assertion and mere denial, as the case may be, on the part of the minister to escape that fact.
Here we are with a cost of living reaching 182 points at the end of April, the highest in our history, and the minister persists in demanding from the house a twenty-five per cent increase in the sales tax. It will not be forgotten, I hope, that in addition to this increase in sales tax a whacking increase in the excise tax on many goods is being imposed as well. These taxes are cumulative. In fact, when you add the tax increase in section 6 of this bill to the tax increases imposed in some of the later sections, you have amazing increases which inevitably will have the effect of increasing very substantially the cost of many of the necessities of life.
Let no one go away with the impression that these taxes have not already had the effect of increasing the cost of many of the commodities to which they apply, and commodities which cannot be said, in a country like ours, measuring the standards of life by established and accepted Canadian standards, to be luxuries. I have before me some figures which I think may be of interest. Electric washers which cost $209 before the minister's budget now sell at $249. An electric iron which cost $14.50 before the budget now sells at $16.50. An electric toaster which cost $9.95 before the budget now costs $11.95. Is that a contribution on the part of the minister to beating down inflation in this country, to making it easier for people to meet the soaring cost of living? You see, the minister can only urge or contend that his increases in these taxes on these commodities, or on the other broad range of commodities to which the sales tax applies, make any contribution toward meeting the problem of inflation, if he goes so far as to say, "I do not want people to buy any of these things. I am going to make it so hard for them to buy these things that they will save their money." And he must go beyond that, and say that it is undesirable that people should have these things.

If the minister says that-and I would like to hear him say it openly and boldly, and not resort to mere general statements which have no evidence to support them- then I think the Canadian public will wish to examine the standard of life the Minister of Finance is proposing to prescribe for them. Have we reached the point where electric toasters are so beyond that scale of living which is regarded as justifiable in Canada that the minister is justified in making this whacking increase in the excise tax, and then this 25 per cent increase in the sales tax as well?
Already the increase in the sales tax has made itself felt. It has already contributed to the increase in the cost of living of the Canadian family. It has already increased to a marked degree the prices of many commodities that are, by all accepted standards, necessities of life. And I am told by people who are in business that this increase in the sales tax has also had a very disturbing effect on methods of doing business, and on the classification of goods in regard to various types of quality and price range. Because this 8 per cent sales tax has been in effect for a long time, it has become a normal even though a very heavy part of the normal cost process, in the production, marketing and sale of goods and commodities.
But the effect of this increase of 25 per cent, from 8 per cent to 10 per cent, added to the mark-ups, and the mark-ups on the mark-ups, and the mark-ups on the mark-ups on the mark-ups, has the effect in a great many cases of pushing goods of a well established classification as to quality and price into an entirely different price range, with the inevitable result that the advance in price to the consumer is going to outrun even the yield in revenue to the government, and the mark-ups in the various hands before they reach the hands of the retailer. That disturbing effect has already made itself felt in marketing with regard to a great many of the basic necessities of life to which this sales tax applies.
You will remember, Mr. Chairman, how in 1935 the late Mr. Mackenzie King, in the election campaign of that year, made the welkin ring with his denunciations of the sales tax, when from coast to coast he denounced it as "that iniquitous tax". You will remember his words, I am sure. It was only 6 per cent then. But in due course he increased it to 8 per cent-and that took place in the first session of parliament after that vitriolic denunciation.
But what is to be said today when, faced with a critical situation in Canada created by inflation, we see the Minister of Finance
Excise Tax Act
proposing another increase in the tax which, at its 6 per cent level, was regarded by the then leader of the Liberal party as an iniquitous tax. I say to you, Mr. Chairman, that there is iniquity written all over this provision in the bill for the increase in the sales tax.
1 will go further and say that, in the face of the way in which business conditions and the cost of living have responded to this increased sales tax, and having regard to the way the cost of living has increased in the interval, and having regard to the sense of public outrage which has attended this proposal and, above all, having regard to the fact that the figures for one month-the month of April-concerning the revenue and expenditure of this country, these have knocked the props completely from under the estimate put before the house by the Minister of Finance as to estimated expenditures and receipts for the whole year. I say that there is no justification remaining now for the Minister of Finance to press this increase in the sales tax upon the people of Canada. And I say that if the government were not so arrogant, if the government were not so everlastingly touchy about any measure of losing face we would see the Minister of of Finance, if he had some realistic appreciation of the burdens of the people of Canada arising from inflation and the soaring cost of living, coming before the House of Commons-and I think the house would applaud him for what would be considered a commendable act upon his part-he would confess, "I think I made some errors. I think I underestimated the extent to which inflation in this country is increasing tax revenue; I think I underestimated the revenues which are going to be yielded by the existing tax. I know that this particular tax, above all others, is inflationary, and that it will abet inflationary forces, and that it will give them increased momentum; and therefore I ask leave of the house to withdraw this section of the bill."

Sometimes I think that had the government deliberately sought some method by which they could aggravate, annoy and anger the Canadian people, they could not have found a better method by which to accomplish that purpose.
During the debate on the budget members of the opposition advanced numerous arguments which, in my opinion, should convince anyone that the government should withdraw this recommendation. We cannot for one moment believe that the government is justified in the light of the fact that the low income groups in the country are finding it increasingly more difficult to purchase the necessities of life. We see no justification for the government pursuing their policy of increasing the sales tax by 25 per cent. We are convinced that there are alternatives. So far as the choice between the personal income tax and the sales tax is concerned, I indicated in my budget speech that I felt under existing conditions an increase in the personal income tax would be inflationary whereas a tax on spending, which does not affect incentives, would not be inflationary. I do not want to traverse all that ground again. If my hon. friend will do me the honour of reading carefully what I said in my budget speech on this subject, and if he will review what I said in the course of the debate on the resolution, I think he will see that I outlined as clearly as I was capable of doing why I felt that it was desirable to spread the load in this way. The Minister of Finance has the unfortunate responsibility-

but it is his responsibility-of deciding what recommendations he will make as to how the total burden must be shared1. I have indicated that. I sincerely believe that the way in which I have endeavoured to apportion the load this year is the fairest and best under the existing circumstances. If I did not think so, I would not have put it forward. I am under no illusion that imposing a sales tax or any ta& is a popular thing to do, but I have the responsibility of trying to determine the best type of tax under existing circumstances, and that is what I have done. I have given the reasons for it to the best of my ability, and there is nothing I can add now to what I have said already.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
I find it difficult to follow the minister's line of reasoning when he suggests that an increase in the income tax would be inflationary but that an increase in the sales tax does not have that effect. As I see it this increase in the sales tax increases the cost of living. It increases it for the people in lower brackets where immediately there is felt the need for larger wages and salaries to meet that increased cost of living. It seems to me that anything that increases the cost of living runs the risk of helping along the spiral of inflation. On the other hand the income tax, particularly if it is applied on a graduated basis with the result that to some degree it is taken from those in the upper brackets, to a large extent cuts down luxury spending and does not have the direct effect in increasing the cost of living that the sales tax certainly has. I am unable to follow the minister in the reasoning that produced the sort of statement he made a moment ago.
I have one other thought to express, and I might as well do it while I am on my feet now. When we have urged as an alternative to the increased sales tax some other taxes such as an increase in the tax on spirituous liquors, for which the hon, member for Springfield voted when I moved an amendment some time ago, or when we have urged that there be increases in the corporation tax, the minister has taken the position that there are times when the point is reached beyond which taxes cannot be increased. His point is that the people concerned just cannot take any further increase in taxation. Well, if he is going to apply that argument to taxes on spirituous liquors and corporations, I would ask him if he does not think the point beyond which further taxation cannot be applied is already reached when the sales tax is at 8 per cent. From the fact that he is raising it to 10 per cent I take it he does not think so, but I believe it would mean something to the
Excise Tax Act
house and the country if we could have an assurance from the minister that it will not go any higher.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I do not want to reopen the debate on the point my hon. friend has raised as to why in the circumstances I think an increase in personal income tax would be more inflationary than a tax on spending. My experience has been that under existing conditions an increase in the income tax means that those paying the increase-and I am referring particularly to the larger groups of organized labour-are not prepared to accept less take-home pay. In other words they feel that they should get a wage increase which would offset any additional tax. I am not going into any elaborate economic argument here, but I make the assertion that unless the over-all production of this country is increased taxes must and should decrease the standard of living in order that a place may be made for the additional defence effort. I have reiterated that time and again. The committee stage is not the time for me to repeat it, but I will say that this is the view of every responsible, competent economist or student of these matters, though I do not offer that as a justification. The tax program I have produced here is the one I believe is best designed, as far as that phase of a fiscal program can do it, to damp down these inflationary forces. I do not claim to be omniscient, as I said before; I may be mistaken, but that does represent my best judgment.
I have answered my hon. friend as to why we think a tax on spending, such as the sales tax, is less inflationary than an increase in the personal income tax or a lowering of the exemptions; because I believe the imposition of such an additional tax would at once result in fairly widespread demands for wage and salary increases to offset it. Under existing conditions a very substantial portion of any such wage increases would be made without any corresponding increase in production, and that is inevitably inflationary. I do not think I have anything else to add; I believe my views are pretty well known. No doubt my hon. friend and others differ with them, but there is really nothing I can add to what I have already said a dozen times.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Does the minister not recognize that an increase in the cost of living makes workers feel that they need higher wages, and rightly so, just as readily as does a loss in take-home pay due to an increase in the income tax?

I think that is a very important point. The minister has put forward two reasons which I do not think hold water. One

Excise Tax Act
is that wage earners are going to demand more money if there is an increase in the income tax. They are going to demand higher wages in exactly the same proportion if the cost of the goods they have to buy is increased by increasing the sales tax. So I do not think that argument holds water. Then the minister said we must decrease the standard of living by increasing the sales tax.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No, I did not. I said if we did not increase production to make up for that $1,700 million defence effort, we must reduce our standard of living. I have said that a dozen times, both in this house and elsewhere.

You do exactly the same thing if you increase the income tax, because in just the same way a man simply does not have the money to spend; it is taken from his income, so what is the difference? My argument and that of other opposition speakers has been that it is much fairer to impose an income tax because the people in the lower income brackets do not pay as much, while those in the higher income brackets pay more because they are better able to pay. Is that not a fair statement?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
That is a matter of opinion.
Perhaps it is unfortunate for the country, but at the moment my hon. friend has not the responsibility of being Minister of Finance. I can only repeat what I said a few moments ago, that I have put forward a program which I honestly believe is the best I have been able to devise. My hon. friend may be right; I do not know. I do not think he is, but I do not suppose either of us will ever convince the other.

I do not think anyone will disagree with the statement that if we are going to increase our expenditures in all kinds of ways, both for social security and for defence, we shall have to increase our production. We all agree with that. Our quarrel is with the form of taxation the minister has adopted.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: We are quarrelling about methods.

I have been waiting for some time to get in a few words. While I have been as opposed to this tax as any man in this house, we all know that in a very short time the government will have to dig up an additional $350 million to provide for the old age pensioners and so on. I am not a member of the government, but I suppose if they did not have a few backbenchers like me around the government would not be here very long. I have had several telephone calls from various quarters suggesting methods of raising money rather than through

the sales tax. As I intimated before, in order to give people an incentive to work we should give them some income tax relief if they produce more than they produced in the previous year. However, the minister and his parliamentary assistant have not seen fit to adopt these suggestions.

That is a pretty good idea,
too.	*

The hon. member for Comox-Alberni is a large income tax payer, and when he approves the suggestion I do not think the idea can be too bad. If the Minister of Finance finds that the increase in the sales tax is not the proper thing to do, then I hope next session he will cancel that increase.

Just so the record will be kept straight, may I remind the hon. member for Springfield that before the new old age pension scheme comes into force he will probably realize that there is to be a new tax imposed for the purpose of financing such a scheme. You wait and see. I was on the committee.

Are all duties on imported goods subject to the ten per cent sales tax? This is one of the greatest injustices of the tax, and there are many injustices. The other day I happened to be getting some goods out of customs for an importer. The duty on the goods brought in from Great Britain amounted to fifty cents per pound. Then on top of that, as the man at the wicket said, you have to pay Abbott's tax of ten per cent. I rather objected to it, and I said I did not think they meant to go into all the crevices for this ten per cent. He said that was the way they interpreted the act, and I would have to pay it. I said that we would have to pass it on to the next fellow who handled these goods. I found that all duties were subject to this ten per cent sales tax.

speechtext: The general rule is that sales tax is on the duty-paid value of the goods, but, of course, there are some exemptions. Therefore, it would not apply to all goods, although they may be subject to duty.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
We disagree, the minister and I, as to this rise from eight to ten per cent. But there is one question that I asked which the minister has not yet answered.

Will the minister not agree that at ten per cent he has reached the maximum to which this sales tax should ever go?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I have always refused to answer hypothetical questions about a rise in taxes. I think it would be most improper for any Minister of Finance to express an opinion in advance that any tax had reached the limit. So long as I have the responsibility, or future ministers of finance have the responsibility, that duty is to try to apportion the burden as fairly as possible. I shall venture no comment as to the maximum level of any tax.

I believe members will be glad to see the procedure provided in this proposed amendment in section 7 relating to the hearings before the tariff board. But I draw attention, Mr. Chairman, to the provision in the proposed new subsection 4 of section 115, which has the effect of limiting to six months the period within which applications for refund may be made. This smacks of the same kind of draftsmanship as we had the other day in a similar provision in the Customs Act dealing with an application for refund where a customs duty had been charged an importer at a higher rate than was proper. In that amending bill it was proposed that the period during which an application for a refund might be made should be reduced from three years to six months. As you will recall, there was a good deal of discussion and an amendment was introduced-in fact, two amendments before the house disposed of the bill.
Now, in this section 7 we have the same kind of proposal that no refund or deduction shall be made under section 105 as the result of any declaration of the tariff board under this section or an order or judgment under section 116 in respect of taxes paid more than six months before the date of the application to the tariff board for a declaration under this section. Mr. Chairman, while feeling that the section, apart from this provision, is improved by the amendment, I urge that the period of six months is unduly restrictive, and that the period within which an application for a refund may be made should be enlarged. I should like to see it enlarged to a year and a half, or certainly not less than twelve months.

Is the government not prepared to enlarge this period of six months? I think you will agree, Mr. Chairman, that six months is a very narrow and brief period of limitation. The decision of the tariff board may be given at a time when the individual concerned is incapacitated for some reason or other. He may be out of the country temporarily. I would urge that a period of six months is an unjustifiably short period of limitation to put upon an application for a refund, where in fact the tariff board has said that an excessively high rate of taxes has been applied or a tax has been applied to an article that is exempt. Under these conditions, it seems to me that the whole-attitude of a government which has collected more taxes than it was entitled to, or has collected taxes where it was not entitled to them, should be one of anxiety to put things right. While the committee I am sure is

Excise Tax Act
commending the general purpose of the amendment, it will want to see this narrow limitation on the period given to that praiseworthy purpose removed or relaxed, so that the period may be a more ample one within which to bring application for a refund.
I would urge that this period of six months be lengthened to not less than twelve months. There is no administrative burden cast upon the Department of National Revenue, surely, by lengthening this period from six months' to twelve months. In a case like this surely we all wish to see right and justice done to a taxpayer who has been required to pay more than he should have, or to make a payment that he should never have been called upon to make, simply because the taxing officer who has had to deal with him has misread the law.
Under these circumstances, Mr. Chairman, I am asking for no great concession on the part of the government in enlarging this undoubtedly short period from six months to twelve months. The Minister of Finance is in the chamber. I urge upon him that the period of six months is altogether too short a period of limitation in a case of this kind. The taxpayer, in the situation I have described, should have no less than twelve months to bring application for a refund.

May I
address a word to the committee before the parliamentary assistant answers? Surely this is a reasonable request, and surely we need not be met with a blanket negation. speechtext:
The Excise Tax Act and of course the Customs Act are quite closely related. Application for refunds would probably apply to both customs duties and excise tax paid on the same goods. of the country neglecting his business completely. The period is much more than six months when you consider the application to the tariff board and the period after the ruling. I am interested in the amendment of section 117, particularly the first subsection. It is to be observed that the limitations in the section as it now stands are eliminated in favour of a provision as broad as this: The minister may designate any person to conduct an inquiry or investigation in matters relating to the act, and any person so appointed has all the power and authority of a commissioner appointed under part I of the Inquiries Act. I ask what has given rise to the proposed amendments, and, in the light of its experience in these matters, in what way the department has found the present section unsatisfactory.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
The effect of this amendment is to limit the carrying out of investigations to persons authorized by the minister, thus removing classes of persons or officers who were formerly empowered to carry out this inquiry by virtue of their office as specified in the act.
The other thing was that no authority was given, similar to part II of the Inquiries Act and the practice on inquiries varied from province to province. It was possible in one province for a person in contempt of inquiry to be sent to prison, and it is to make sure that there is a uniform practice in all ten provinces that this clause, which is again exactly similar to the clause in the customs bill amending the Customs Act passed here ten days ago, was incorporated.

The parliamentary assistant has not grasped the point that I was raising about this. The terms of the present section 116 are, in many respects, narrower than the provisions of the new proposed section 117, subsection 1. The persons who may be designated as a commissioner under the present

legislation are-limited to the deputy minister of the department, the assistant deputy minister, the legal officer or -any other officer authorized by the minister from time to time. The effect of the substituted provision, the new section 117, subsection 1, is to enlarge that clause without limit. The minister may appoint any person. I am asking, what has given rise to the apparent feeling that the present class, as drawn from within the ranks of the department, is too narrow and that the minister should have power to appoint any person as a commissioner to carry out the functions which may be assigned to such a person under the act with the powers and authority of a commissioner appointed under part I of the Inquiries Act.

Officer.

Excise Tax Act

I should

The proviso at the top of page seven indicates another discriminatory feature of the tax. It states that the tax shall apply only to that portion of the appliance designed for other than solid fuels. Certain appliances will be subject to the tax while other appliances, such as stoves using a different type of fuel, will not be subject to the tax. That is necessarily discriminatory. It brings us back to this question: If the minister does need revenue, why should a particular industry like this be singled out for a tax which is not general in application but which in its result is highly discriminatory?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
As far as the first point
raised by the hon. member for Eglinton is concerned, the addition of the words "or apartment" in paragraph (a) is made necessary because of the new paragraph (b). In paragraph (b) the words "appliances adapted to household or apartment use" are used. The easy phrase would be "domestic use". However, in many apartments the refrigerator system is made up of one compressor in the basement with a refrigerator unit in each apartment. Obviously such an appliance would not be covered by the word "household". It would not be covered by the words "domestic use." The expression was expanded

Excise Tax Act
to "household or apartment use" in paragraph (b), and for the sake of uniformity the same expression was used in paragraph (a).
Then as to why this special tax should be imposed. There are two reasons for this. The minister gave the first reason when delivering his budget speech, and I also emphasized that when I spoke. The primary purpose is to raise revenue, to make possible our defence preparations and to provide the domestic services of the federal government.
There was a second purpose, as the minister indicated. These taxes were intended to have a counter-inflationary effect where there was an element of competition with defence industry. The hon. member for Eglinton mentioned the automobile industry, but if there is one industry where there is a high element of competition with our defence industry, it is the electrical industry. This is true not only with regard to the use of materials such as iron and steel, but particularly so in the case of copper. I used a striking illustration of the Anaconda Copper Company and the amount of copper necessary to construct a tank or a bomber as compared to the amount used in an ordinary kitchen. In this particular instance we have real competition both in materials and in the type of labour necessary to produce the many electronic devices used in war.
Then with regard to the exemption of appliances designed to use solid fuels, may I say that these were exempted during the last war. Coal or wood stoves are used generally in farming and outlying areas. We followed the same taxation policy in the last war, although with higher rates of taxation. In connection with these combination stoves we determine the electrical content of the stove as distinguished from what you would call the ordinary coal or wood part. We are now carrying out exactly the same provision today as we did when a similar tax was applied during the war. This action was explained at some considerable length during the resolution stage.

There is one special point. In raising it I do not wish to distract attention from the main feature here which is the question whether there should be a tax on these articles at all. In both 3(a) and 3(b) we have a provision which opens in general terms and then follows with a detailed enumeration preceded by the abbreviation "viz.". I notice that section 3(a) reads:
Electrical appliances adapted to household or apartment use, viz. . . .

Then follows the enumeration, chafing dishes, coffee makers, and so on. In 3(b) we have a similar expression. It reads:
Appliances adapted to household or apartment use, viz., stoves, hot plates, grills and other appliances ...	[DOT]
I think there is a point of interpretation that ought to be cleared up at this stage. Does the Department of National Revenue propose to apply this schedule with this effect, that the enumeration is not necessarily exhaustive, but if they can find anything that falls within the definition of electrical appliances adapted to household or apartment use it becomes taxable even though it is not one of the particular articles singled out in the enumeration that follows? The same question arises in 3(b). If these articles are simply set out here for the purpose of illustration or example one would have expected the abbreviation "e.g.". I have not seen the French version of the bill. It may be that it will throw some light on the question. As I understand it, "viz." is an abbreviation of videlicet, and it has not the same meaning at all as "e.g." or exempli gratia. What is the interpretation that the department is going to place on this expression? In other words, are the governing words going to be the opening and general words or are they going to be the specific enumerations which follow the general words? I can well imagine that no matter how carefully the draftsman may have sought to set out a very detailed enumeration, he may not have covered everything in the way of electrical appliances concerning which an attempt may later be made to apply the tax.
I have now been handed the French version, and see that 3(a) reads as follows:
Appareils et materiel electriques adaptes a l'usage de maisons ou appartements, soit couvertures; chauffe-plat . . .
Similarly in 3(b) it reads, "soit cuisinieres". After the general words we have the one word, "soit".

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: The intention is to carry on the practice of the department up until now, and that is indicated by the use of the word "soit" with these specific articles mentioned here. If they are not mentioned they are not going to be covered, with one exception. If the hon. member will look at 3(b) there is one fairly general class, "stoves, hot plates, grills and other appliances when adapted wholly or in part for cooking". If some new method of cooking were devised then it could be included under this one omnibus section, but otherwise the items specified are the items on which the tax will be collected, and items not specified will not be taxed.

Is that a solemn assurance from the parliamentary assistant on behalf of the government that this section will not be applied to any electrical appliance adapted to household or apartment use unless that particular article is specified in the detailed enumeration that follows "viz."?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: That has been the practice of the department, and that will continue to be the practice with the one exception of this blanket clause in 3(b) as far as cooking appliances are concerned.

To what other cooking appliances could that particular clause apply other than stoves, hot plates, or grills when adapted wholly or in part for cooking and when designed for using other than solid fuels? What appliances could that refer to?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: As an example of development, you will remember that four or five years ago they brought out these little electric portable roasters which actually they advertised as complete outfits for small apartments. That type of thing is an example of development that may take place. We may well have a similar development so far as cooking stoves are concerned, and it is to cover that. Aside from that, the practice of the department has been that the article must be specified. If it is specified here it is taxed. If it is not specified here, then there is no 25 per cent or 15 per cent excise tax.

What is the significance of
the words "adapted to household or apartment use"? Does that mean that restaurants, hotels and so on will be exempt from this tax?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes, the article is part of the cost of production.

You consider that to be
like tools of the industry.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is right.

They would be exempt
from taxation.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Correct.

The hon. member for Eglinton attacked the tax from the point of view of the manufacturers of electrical appliances. I should like to go to the other end and say a word for the consumer. I am opposed to this tax to the degree that it militates against the introduction of labour-saving devices in the home. I want to say a word particularly about washing machines under 3 (b). It refers to "washing machines operated by electric or other power". So far as the words "other power" are concerned, I am thinking
Excise Tax Act
about manpower, human power. Unfortunately it is not manpower. It is woman-power in a great many homes, and that is what I am thinking about. I am thinking of the wife in the farm home, or in the city or town home for that matter. It appears to me that this is a drive against the installation of modern labour-saving devices.
In the province of Saskatchewan, with a widely scattered population, we have had considerable success in the matter of electrification. It has been slow but we have made a start. Many women are looking forward to the day when they can have electric lights, and when they will not have to push that handle back and forth for an hour or two every time they wash.
Use that $65 million for that.

1 think the government should be encouraging rather than discouraging the installation of such devices. I think taxation on such articles will be a bitter disappointment to the people about whom I am most concerned. I can see no single justification for this particular tax unless it is on the ground of the amount of steel that will be saved for the country in what is considered by many to be an emergency. I do not think the amount of steel that will be saved on that one item is going to be very great in relationship to the vast quantity of steel that may be needed. I can see no justification for this tax. As long as a woman will push that handle all day long in the heat of a little kitchen in order to wash her clothes, it is quite all right, but let her go get her husband to hook up her washing machine to a little gasoline engine, or let her use the electrification to which they have been looking forward for years, and the government comes along and says: All right, if you want to instal that particular type of machine you will have to pay for it as if it were a luxury. I think the washing machine item should be deleted from this particular clause.

Yesterday or the day before the Canadian Manufacturers Association met in Montreal, and the president made a statement that I thought was at least significant. He stated that so far as these appliances were concerned the slack in consumer demand was not being taken up by armament orders from the government. Mr. Holding, who is the president, made this statement:
Yet except for a few selected industries such as the manufacture of airplanes and railroad equipment, I have seen little evidence that rearmament

Excise Tax Act
production will take up the slack in the employment of labour, plant and equipment which will be released1 by the curtailment in production of consumer goods.
So I am beginning to wonder. Obviously we do not have this tax for revenue; at least that is not its main purpose, in view of the surplus we had in the first month. It cannot be designed to conserve steel and other materials, because we are not using for defence production the steel and other materials we are saving by reducing the manufacture of consumer appliances. In the light of those facts exactly where do we stand? Is it still necessary? I would like the parliamentary assistant or the minister to tell me whether in recent weeks any manufacturers have made representations to the department that they are going to have unemployment in their industries if this provision is continued.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
Getting back once again to the primary purpose, that purpose was to raise revenue. In his budget speech the minister drew attention to the amazing rate of spending which had developed in recent years in connection with these articles. The example which sticks in my mind is refrigerators. The 1950 sales were double those of 1949 and three times those of 1948. I put the figures for automobiles on record previously, and the minister has said that the March sales of new cars amounted to 49,000 units. Everyone forecast that there would be a collapse in sales after the budget. Very early in April the hon. member for Peterborough West predicted a total collapse in automobile sales once these tax changes went through. In spite of the anticipatory buying in March by people who normally would have waited until April or May, the sales in April amounted to 46,300 new cars, so that is not much evidence of a collapse. Exactly the same thing is true as far as these items are concerned. The hon. member asks if these increased taxes, and I suppose he would also include the credit restrictions, have resulted in unemployment. He also asks whether the steel, copper and other materials which have been made available by the reduced sales-though as far as the government can see the sales have not been reduced very much-have been turned to war purposes. Well, war purposes or no, there is no surplus of either steel or copper in this country today.
To reply to the hon. member for Saskatoon, on the budget resolutions, the hon. member for Peace River asked whether this other power meant manpower, and I said it did not. The case brought forward was that of a farmer in Saskatchewan who has been operating a hand washing machine. He has

his farm electrified and wants to buy a little motor and hitch it up to the old washing machine. Well, the Department of National Revenue will not go to his farm and say, "Now you have an electric machine." But if he goes to the store and buys a new electric washing machine, of course he comes under this tax.

Anyone in his right senses knows that you cannot hitch electricity to an old hand type washing machine. If there is some genius on the farm you might be able to get gasoline power on that washer, but everyone knows that electrification involves the purchase of a new electrical machine. I think the parliamentary assistant is over-simplifying the case.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: I certainly am not oversimplifying that case. I have a very large rural riding, too, to which electrification is coming, and I am always amazed at the ingenuity shown by the farmers and fishermen in adapting things from the old manual processes to electrification. However, that is a minor thing.
They could live in sod houses, too.

The parliamentary assistant
mentioned that I had spoken about cars and said they would be a drug on the market. I believe he will bear me out when I say that most manufacturers of cars in Canada have those cars out in fields by the hundred, unable to get rid of them, and every car dealer across the country has used cars he cannot sell.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Both manufacturers and dealers have been doing very well for the last four or five years. There was perhaps some anticipation of possible tax increases before the budget was brought down, and there might have been some inclination to stimulate manufacturers to load up the dealers. I would not know too much about that, but I do not think the situation is very serious as yet as far as either the manufacturers or the dealers are concerned.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: A few moments ago the parliamentary assistant indicated to the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar that a distinction is made between those appliances which are used domestically and the same appliances used in restaurants, hotels and so on. I should like to know whether for the distinction to be made it has to be a different type of stove or washing machine, or whether it is the case that a stove purchased for the home is subject to tax whereas the same stove purchased for a restaurant is not.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
The normal practice for a restaurant certainly would not be to buy the

ordinary type of stove adapted to household or apartment use. They would buy a stove of a different size, much bigger, and adapted to restaurant or other commercial use. The same would apply to a refrigerator. If the stove is of a type adapted to household use, the ordinary small household electric stove, and it is bought for use in a restaurant the tax would apply, because it would be a stove adapted to household or apartment use. The stoves and refrigerators used by ordinary restaurants and hotels are very different in character from those used in homes.

In a good many modern
apartment blocks they have Bendix washers which are operated by putting a quarter in the slot, or something of that sort. Would they come under this, since they would be adapted to apartment use? On the other hand within perhaps a block or two of the apartment you may have one of these washeterias, with the same type of machine also operated by putting a quarter in the slot. The apartment house owner put in the machines largely as a service to the occupants of the block, while of course the other people are running a business. Would there be a distinction between those identical machines, both operated by money in the slot but one placed in the basement of an apartment and the other in a building next door called a washeteria?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: The tax is levied when the manufacturer sells to the wholesaler. He does not know where the washing machine is going, whether it is going into one of these small washeterias on the main street or into an apartment. In the apartment, of course, it is obviously adapted to apartment use, the same as the refrigerator. In the case of the small washeteria it is a washing machine adapted to household use, and it pays the sales and excise taxes when the manufacturer sells it to the wholesaler. On the other hand some people make much larger washing machines which are not adapted to household use but which are used by commercial laundries, and of course they are exempt from the excise tax.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Then the test is not who finally purchases the article but the way it is constructed, or what it is adapted for?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Yes, what it is commonly used for.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Does the parliamentary
assistant not fear that in this tax he is discriminating against those people who like to eat at home?

If a person had something go wrong with his refrigerator and had to buy a new freezing unit, would the 25 per cent tax apply?

This is the paragraph under
which the excise tax is increased from 15 per cent to 25 per cent on trunks, suitcases, baggage and luggage of all kinds. Mr. Chairman, it is surely a great mistake to base any tax on the assumption that luggage of all kinds is necessarily a luxury. Even if additional revenue is required I believe we must have some regard, especially in times like this, to avoid increasing the cost of things that are necessities of life. In certain cases luggage is undoubtedly a necessity. Now, I would have been quite prepared to accept without question the necessity for a tax on some of the articles enumerated in paragraph 8, if some serious attempt had been made to distinguish between those that are of utility quality and those that are of luxury quality. There is no attempt of that kind made here at all. I wish to record my feeling that there is a grave injustice being done here to a particular industry, the leather goods industry, when there is not the slightest attempt made to distinguish between those forms of goods which are luxuries and those which are necessities.

I should
like to support what the member for Eglinton has said. I have always felt that in the case of the tax on leather goods, there is no rhyme or reason whatever. In a good many of the other cases I think I can see some reason, but here it seems to me there is a clear case for making a distinction. Presumably it would have to be made on the basis of cost or something of that kind, but no attempt has ever been made to do it.

I agree with the two previous
speakers, but I think there is a distinction made here. There is a distinction made in the case of articles specially manufactured for a customer, and in that case it would be the better class of goods. If you are a wealthy individual and can afford to have something

Excise Tax Act
specially made, you are exempt from taxation. But if it is a necessity and you have to go to an ordinary store to purchase it, you are subject to the tax. I believe the section is wrong.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: The distinction is so reasonable. If a doctor wants to buy a little black bag for his instruments or a travelling salesman wants a bag specially made to hold his goods, then he comes within this section and the goods are exempt from taxation. The tax is progressive so far as income is concerned, too. For instance, take the old age pensioner who travels to see his daugther. He buys a small cardboard suitcase, for say three dollars, and the excise tax he pays in that cost is less than 75 cents. On the other hand a rich man who goes down to Florida from Toronto to escape Toronto's winter probably has pigskin cases costing $500, so he has to pay a heavy tax under the twenty-five per cent rate. This is a good example. The higher the income group in which you are, the fancier your luggage and the higher tax you pay because of the twenty-five per cent rate.

The words "manufactured
expressly for" should be removed, because a young man starting in business cannot afford to have luggage specially manufactured. He has to purchase it on the open market. If the exception were for suitcases and briefcases used for business purposes, then I could see the point. When the words "manufactured expressly for" are used, that excludes the man who has to buy the cheaper type of travelling case and briefcase. The man who could well afford to pay the tax in this case is exempted.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
This item should not pass with the explanation that has been given. It will pass, there is no doubt about that. But this explanation is just as specious as the explanation that was given for the tax on electrical equipment. On the one hand, we are told it is for revenue, and on the other hand we are told it is to cut production. No real facts have been given to demonstrate that either is the case. In this particular case the parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Finance has given one of those wholly specious illustrations about the rich man carrying the big leather case. As a matter of fact, he will probably find that those who are doing the kind of travelling he is talking about have adopted other kinds of cases.
In this particular instance the provision is not fair. Those who are in a position to get any of these things specially made are exempted, and those who are not must go in and buy the ordinary manufactured article

on which the tax is imposed. This is certainly going to pass, according to the attitude that is being adopted; there is no doubt about it. We see the same attitude right down the line: Who is going to stop us? But let us not pass this item with the idea that we are accepting the kind of explanation that has been given.

I should like to support the previous speakers. Upon looking over the list it seems to me that purses, wallets, billfolds, key and card cases, dressing and toilet cases, shopping bags, golf and other sport bags, expressly manufactured for a customer, are the height of luxury and should be subject to tax.

Fountain pens are capable of being divided into those categories that may be regarded as luxuries and those that are strictly and unquestionably necessities. As for the latter type, surely no one is going to say that they are not a necessity of life. Why should they be singled out for a discriminatory tax?
