speechtext: The house resumed from Friday, May 25, consideration of the motion of Mr. Robinson, for the second reading of Bill No. 118, to incorporate Border Pipeline Corporation, and the proposed amendment thereto of Mr. Herridge.

When this bill was under consideration previously I moved the adjournment of the debate. At that time I spoke in favour of the amendment, and I am going to repeat my reason for doing so. We in British Columbia, and by that I mean practically 95 per -cent of the people of that province, have taken the stand that these pipe lines should pass through Canada. This particular company has not seen fit to incorporate in the bill a clause to that effect, and through the amendment we are seeking to have that provision inserted. I am sure if the sponsor of the bill would agree to incorporate a clause under which this pipe line would serve Canadian cities first, any objection on my part would be withdrawn immediately.
I pointed out also that we are now faced with a greater need than ever before to consider the conservation of our natural resources. Already in the United States, through lack of any sound conservation policy, they find themselves running out of many raw materials for which they are now looking to Canada. Unless we have a policy, and unless we check what is taking place, we also will find ourselves in the unhappy position the United States is in, having to -come to Canada for pulpwood and other raw materials. So I advocate that as part of that conservation policy the government should step in right now and support the conservation of our gas and oil in Alberta. I feel that this would pay dividends, for the amount paid for our raw materials, whether they be ore, timber, oil or gas, by our neighbour to the south is very small compared to the value of those materials if processed in Canada. In addition, this cheap power we are going to provide the United States will assist our greatest competitor to become even more competitive, which naturally will react unfavourably upon our own industry. I strongly feel that we should process our own raw materials instead of exporting them at nominal prices. Already we have a top-heavy balance of trade in favour of the United

Border Pipeline Corporation States, and that balance will be further intensified if we do not follow a policy of conservation.
I am not opposed to the United States obtaining some of our surplus gas, but I am opposed to that country having the first chance to use that gas. If we should run short, or if the expected amount should not be available, then Vancouver and other Canadian points would get none at all. There is no suggestion by those sponsoring this bill that they intend to serve any other Canadian point but Vancouver. As far as British Columbia is concerned Vancouver is just one point. We have a vast interior thirsting for this power and just as anxious to have it as Vancouver. I mention Vancouver because under this charter it is the only point in Canada this company intends to serve. I have already indicated the vast resources of the hinterland, the type of people living there, the climate we enjoy, and the new era that will dawn if we are given this power to develop our resources. I do not intend to stand idly by and watch this particular resource be sabotaged from under our feet. At least we can register our protest.
The main argument advanced by these companies for going through the United States is the lack of markets on the Canadian route. On checking a map of the route proposed in this case I find that in going through the United States it would serve only Spokane before reaching the Pacific coast. Calgary could be served by a short line at any time, and I believe a short pipe line serving Calgary would be a very profitable undertaking.

I must admit that I am not very familiar with the geography of British Columbia, but am I not correct in saying that this pipe line will pass through the Kootenay district, one of the greatest industrial areas of the province?
You should know; you are sponsoring the bill. My answer would be no.
Is not the Kootenay district a great industrial area?

No, Kingsgate. I am referring to the Okanagan valley, the Fraser valley and Kamloops, all those towns in the interior. This line will not go through the Trail area. It will go close to it, and probably will be piped in; I do not know. It is intended to go through Kingsgate, which takes it directly to Spokane.
The rail transportation costs for oil, for instance, from central Alberta to Calgary, a matter of 200 miles, is 65 to 68 cents per
'Mr. Jones.]
barrel. The Interprovincial Pipe Line carrying oil 1,150 miles to the great lakes carries it for 56 cents per barrel. I claim, therefore, that the loss of the Spokane consumers to the pipe-line company would be recovered by the gross of the British Columbia interior towns, particularly the valleys I mentioned and the communities that occupy those valleys. Furthermore, the towns of Nelson and Trail, and this big consumer to whom I referred, the Consolidated Smelters, could be served if the pipe line followed the route through southern British Columbia instead of going through the United States.
It seems to me we are entirely overlooking the potential value of the pipe line as a developing influence in our country's economy. We have stressed the importance of the money to be made by the sale of gas and oil, and not the wealth that can be made by utilizing that gas and oil in our own country to increase our own production. The government has been asking for more production, but will not channel the power to sources that could provide this extra production. I believe that the pipe line should be built, owned and operated by the government, but unfortunately that point has been settled. I believe it should be run as the Canadian National is run, and by the same company. It could have been added as another form of transportation to the already operating transportation system. Whether it is a railway, the T.C.A. or a pipe line should make no difference.
Since a pipe line is the only feasible means of transporting gas or oil to the Pacific coast, and possibly only one pipe line will be built, it follows that the company building the line will have a complete monopoly. This means that they will control not only the line but also the price to be paid by the consumer for the product. In the United States, where a similar condition existed, they have passed a law to remedy this condition. I should like to quote from the work of Mr. Sharfman, the interstate commerce commission, 1931, part II, at page 59:
"The acquisition of a practical pipe-line monopoly by the Standard Oil Company, together with the unfair methods pursued by that corporation in order to maintain its monopolistic position, led to the inclusion of pipe lines among the carriers subject to the commission's jurisdiction. Although the commission was clothed with authority, in general terms, over any additional transportation agency, the extension of jurisdiction was largely aimed against the abuses of monopolistic power in the petroleum industry rather than against the free operation of pipe lines as such. By 1906 the commission possessed adequate power to remove the flagrant railroad discriminations of which the Standard Oil Company had been one of the most notorious beneficiaries: the added control over pipe lines was designed to eliminate another potent

source of abuse which sprang from that company's dominant ownership of essential transportation facilities."
By the Natural Gas Act, 1938, it is provided that all rates and charges made, demanded or received by any natural gas company for the transportation or sale of natural gas, must be just and reasonable, and any rate which is not just and1 reasonable is declared to be unlawful (section 4 (a)). Discrimination is expressly prohibited, it being provided that no natural gas company may "make or grant any undue preference or advantage to any person or subject any person to any undue prejudice or disadvantage." Unreasonable differences in rates, charges, services, facilities, and in other respects between localities or classes of services are prohibited (section 4 (b)). The act provides for the fixing of rates by the federal power commission according to fair and equitable principles (section 5 (a)). It may act upon its own motion, or upon application of any interested persons, including state commissions which may be of opinion that rates or conditions in particular instances are discriminatory or unfair. By this machinery, gas pipe lines falling within the term "interstate commerce" are controllable.
At present there is no corresponding act in operation in Canada. I would urge that the government, for the protection of consumers, study this act with a view to incorporating it in our own laws. Naturally, I am concerned over the fact one company is going to obtain a charter to build the pipe line, although there are many applicants at present. I would suggest that the government should give consideration now to passing laws to protect the consuming public against any tendency on the part of such a company to exercise the monopoly it would have to the detriment of the people of my province. Naturally, the price would be based on the principle of what the market would bear. I consider this company, like the others who have applied for a charter, has evinced a desire for quick profit, and has put that above the interests of the Canadian people. I make no apology, therefore, when I place the interests of my own riding and; my own province before the welfare of any particular company. I not only do so, but I would ask the members on the other side who are shouting, the members from the other provinces, to see the point the members from British Columbia are trying to place before you, that we are trying to build our own province now before it is too late. In a year's time it will be too late. We shall see the state of Washington going ahead and will realize what could have happened in British Columbia.
When I speak on this bill I want you to understand that I have nothing against the company, nothing against the directors, and nothing against the sponsor of the bill. I merely object to a bill being passed by a vast majority of people who do not know the conditions, and which would react to the detriment of the people I am representing.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to make a few observations at this point. Of course it is obvious that the detailed discussion will be under the sections of the bill, but I should like to say a word or two about a point which arises many times in the bill. I refer to the practice, which seems to me to be growing, of retroactive legislation. I have had an examination made of the bill, and as it stands there are two cases where it is made retroactive to 1948, seven cases where it is made retroactive to 1949 and subsequent years, seven cases where it is made retroactive to 1950 and subsequent years, and twelve cases where it is made retroactive to the beginning of 1951. Let me say quickly that I am not laying great stress on the last twelve cases, and I also want to say that in a considerable number of other cases I think the retroactive feature is in the nature of a relieving provision.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Every case, I think.

Naturally I take no objection to those, but there are some -and I will not attempt to say how many at the moment-which I think are objectionable. I want to say a word or two about the question of retroactive legislation and to quote briefly one authority on it. The authority to whom I wish to refer is Professor C. K.
Income Tax Act
Allen, sometime professor of jurisprudence in the university of Oxford. He says:
No rule of construction is more firmly established than this: that a retrospective operation is not to be given to a statute so as to impair an existing right or obligation, otherwise than as regards matter of procedure, unless that effect cannot be avoided without doing violence to the language of the enactment. If the enactment is expressed in language which is fairly capable of either interpretation, it ought to be construed as prospective only.
Then he goes on, and this is my precise point:
What is true of the construction of statutes is also true of their making. There is in all civilized states the strongest prejudice against retrospective or ex post facto legislation, since it is, in the words of Willes J., "prima facie of questionable policy, and contrary to the general principle that legislation by which the conduct of mankind is to be regulated ought, when introduced for the first time, to deal with future acts, and ought not to change the character of past transactions carried on upon the faith of the then existing law."
I want to point out that I think the evil of this kind of legislation is not merely the great danger there is that it does injustice to existing situations but also that I think it promotes carelessness in the drafting of legislation. If the legislative draftsmen have the feeling that if they overlook anything, or deal in a superficial way with anything, it is all right because they will cure it next year, the year after, or three or four years after, I think that is a very undesirable situation.
There is one other point I wish to make, though I do this with some hesitation and certainly not with the intention of being critical of any of our excellent civil servants. In reading legislation I have often wondered whether we are not slipping into a terribly complicated way of expressing ourselves. I realize that legal draftsmanship is a very difficult thing, that it has to be specific and exact; but with deference I do raise the question whether we are not falling into rather a bad tradition under which things are not said in a direct way but constantly tend to be said in an indirect and rather confusing way so that sometimes one rather feels one has to turn himself inside out two or three times before getting to the real meaning of the statute. That may be very good for the lawyers, but it is not good for the ordinary people who have to try to understand the legislation as they go along.
Those were the observations I wished to make. I understand that when we reach section 1 of the bill in committee we shall be able to raise the question of deferred depreciation which was dealt with by the minister in his budget speech.

But when a C.C.F. party member differs with his colleagues, perhaps once in fifty times, it is a party split or a rift or a disagreement

on a fundamental issue; or it is heresy, or kicking over the traces.
I want to say that this party is just as democratic an organization as the Liberal party, indeed much more so. My own leader, the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell), rose just after I differed some weeks ago and made this statement:
One of the greatest strengths of a democratic organization is of course that there can be differences of opinion expressed freely and openly.
My party colleagues do not object if I differ with them once in a while. They may think I am wrong, but they have not tried to suppress me at all. I have heard the hon. Liberal member for Fraser Valley (Mr. Cruickshank) differ with his party on margarine. I have heard the hon. member for Temiscouata (Mr. Pouliot) differ with his party on numerous occasions. I do not think my constituents expect me to come down here and vote in a way I do not think is correct. For instance, I do not think they would want me to do what the hon. member for Springfield (Mr. Sinnott) did this afternoon; that is, say he was against a tax and then vote for it. That does not make sense to me. As I say, since coming down here I have tried to vote according to the way I saw the issue.
I am very proud of the C.C.F. party. I am proud to be a member, and I intend to continue to be a member. I think they are doing an excellent job in Saskatchewan despite what is being said in the Liberal press. I like their hospitalization plan, their crown corporations, their financial achievements, their labour legislation, and just about everything else they have done. These Sifton papers are so biased that many people are beginning to take what they read in them with a grain of salt. According to the Sifton papers everything the Liberal party does is perfect, but there is something wrong with everything the C.C.F. party does. That does not make sense, and I say editorial comments of that kind are unwarranted, unfair and at times even malicious. As a matter of fact I consider myself a very good C.C.F. member; I think I am a good deal further to the left than many of my colleagues.
Then there is another point. I am getting a little tired of hearing my good friends in the Liberal party claim that in order to be a C.C.F. member you have to be either broke or crazy. As a matter of fact some members of the Labour party in England are among the wealthiest people in that country. I resent some of the innuendos that have been thrown around in this house and in some of the newspapers of western Canada. I apologize for having been personal, Mr. Speaker, and I will not take up more of the

time of the house. For the benefit of the Leader-Post, however, I want to repeat that I have no thought of resigning from the C.C.F. and no one in this party has suggested that I should resign.

I should like to comment briefly upon several matters during this debate on second reading. In view of the understanding which I believe has been arrived at that the subject of depreciation will be discussed on the first section in committee, I say nothing on that point.
In introducing his budget on April 10 the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) indicated that in devising his tax proposals for this year he had started from this premise, as he stated at page 1807 of Hansard:
It is generally agreed, I think, that we have an excellent basic tax structure.
While there are limitations upon a discussion of the basic tax structure on a bill of this kind, I do hope an opportunity is going to be provided soon for consideration by the house of what I consider to be the quite inadequate provisions in our income tax laws in relation to exemptions. Certain exemptions there have been won by progressive degrees, but I think the list is quite inadequate. Having regard to the increased expenditure at the present time it may be that the minister will not be very receptive to suggestions for broadening certain exemptions and extending them to categories not now provided in the act, but I do hope an opportunity for considering such questions will be afforded before very long.
I am sorry that when the debate on the budget resolutions concluded the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) did not have something to say on a matter which was touched upon by him in his budget speech, and was referred to by several members during the course of the debate. It is the subject of savings. At page 1803 of Hansard for April 10 the minister stated:
There is also urgent need for a higher volume of new savings . . .
Further on the same page:
The important thing is to achieve an increase in aggregate saving up to a level at least equal to the new capital investment which we shall have to make this year.
Now, others commented on this, as I did. I sought to draw the attention of the minister-

I referred to his recognition of the importance of savings, Mr. Speaker, and I mentioned, as I did earlier, that the new taxes which the Minister of Finance is asking the house to vote, much of them in the present bill, will amount to $625 million. Last year, the total savings in Canada amounted to $645 million, which represented a decrease of thirty per cent as compared with the year before. Now, if there is not an expansion of national savings effort this year, it means that with these additional taxes the volume of savings in Canada will drop to a mere $20 million, and that would be calamitous.
I commend the statement made on this subject at the annual meeting of the

Income Tax Act
Dominion Mortgage and Investment Association in Montreal on May 3, by the president of that association, Mr. H. E. Langford of Toronto, who said:
As we all know, inflation is the great problem we face. To overcome it, all the weapons available to us must be used. One of the most effective weapons is savings . . .
Then after giving some examples, he adds: . . . one of the major battles against inflation will be lost if the rate of savings is not maintained or even increased. The need of individuals for larger savings than ever before is readily apparent. Helping individual Canadians along this road will be profitable not only to them and ourselves, but will assist in the over-all struggle against depreciation of the dollar.
It is considerations of that kind, Mr. Speaker, that have guided some of us in what we have had to say, not only on this present measure but on other budget measures that have lately been before the house.
There is one other matter which I hope there will be an opportunity to discuss adequately on this bill. It does not arise in the bill, but it arises out of orders in council which have accompanied the bill. I refer to the matter of the increase in the percentage of deduction which employers are required to hold back from their employees out of wages or salaries on account of income tax. The attempt to increase these deductions to make them cover one hundred per cent of the tax is going to give rise to a multiplicity of claims for refunds. When people come to make their returns on April 30, and to take account of their charitable donations or their medical expenses, claims for refunds will arise. I believe that is a step too far, and it is going to create inconvenience for many people in having to apply for refunds and await payment of them.

Mr. Speaker, the previous speaker sat down rather more quickly than I expected. I wish to make a few brief remarks on the second reading of this bill, because it is of great importance to the members of this group and the people of Canada, particularly in connection with certain aspects of the Income Tax Act, as we take a somewhat different view than many other members in- this house. Now, Mr. Speaker, I believe we can agree with the late Mr. Justice Holmes in respect of the payment of income tax. He is described as having paid his income tax with alacrity instead of anguish because he said, "With this I always buy civilization." We can agree with that outlook in respect to income tax when fairly levied.
As I said before, Mr. Speaker, in speaking on the resolution preceding the bill, the

C.C.F. group considers that the necessary revenue could be more fairly raised without the imposition of the surtax on the lower income groups. I am particularly speaking now of those married people with incomes of $3,000 a year or less, and single people with incomes of $1,500 a year or less. It is a basic principle with the C.C.F. movement that taxation should be based on the ability to pay. We take objection to certain aspects of this bill because we believe that principle is violated. Therefore, in what I say this evening I am speaking for this group, and expressing the considered opinion of the C.C.F. party to which I belong.
I wish to illustrate briefly our contention-

speakerposition: Speaker of the Senate
speechtext:
Order. Probably I should bring to the hon. member's attention the fact that on the motion for the house to go into committee of ways and means, an amendment was voted upon which reads as follows:
The house further regrets the failure of the government to exempt from the proposed twenty per cent defence surtax, the incomes of single persons up to $1,500 and the incomes of married persons up to $3,000.
That question was decided this year, and I doubt if a debate on that matter should be revived at this time. I would not object to the hon. member making a brief statement, but I would not want him to enter into a long discussion on that.

Mr. Speaker, you are quite correct. I only mentioned those facts in passing, and was not really discussing that question on this occasion. I wish to briefly illustrate our contention that large corporation profits are, in our opinion, a more just source of revenue than the revenue which is received or will be received from certain groups at this time. Since we last dealt with this question there has been increasing evidence in support of our argument. There is an accumulation of evidence in support of the point of view presented by the members of this group.
I am not going to speak at length, but I do just want to illustrate that point before proceeding to give my conclusions. I hold in my hand a clipping from the Financial Post of May 26. Whether we agree with the financial policies of the Financial Post or not, we do know it is an accurate and reliable report of business development, business profits and all things connected with business activity at this time. I think its records and its statistical information have been unquestioned. Throughout the years this paper has proven to be extremely reliable as a source of information with respect to business developments.
I notice in this paper some reference to the increasingly improved position of large

corporations in this country; therefore I intend to quote briefly from it. I am simply using this as a source of information. I am not quoting it editorially but as a source of statistical information because of its validity and soundness in supporting our arguments. This article says:
Canadian business had a good year on the average in 1950. The combined profit of 362 Canadian business firms for 1950 was up 23-8 per cent from their 1949 net. Over 69 per cent of these companies showed a higher net in 1950 than in 1949.
I want hon. members to just think of that when they are thinking of the requests for increasing the basic disability pension for veterans when next those requests come before the house. I am coming back into order, Mr. Speaker. I continue:
Further the combined financial position of these companies was strengthened. Net working capital of the 362 companies increased 18-3 per cent during the year and their net worth (equity of all shareholders) increased 9-1 per cent. Thus they improved their position for meeting the demands of the defence economy and for weathering any adverse economic conditions that may lie ahead.
The article goes on to say:
Some significant facts disclosed by the Post's study are:
(1)	Total income taxes paid by 360 of these firms were 34-8 per cent higher in 1950 than in 1949. This reflects both the increased volume of business and resultant higher earnings and the increase of 5 per cent in the rate of tax effective after September 1, 1950.
(2)	Shareholders received 22 per cent more in total dollar dividends in 1950 than in 1949. The percentage increase in dividends paid was only slightly less than the percentage increase in net profit.
(3)	Despite the increase in cash dividends paid, shareholders of these firms received a smaller proportion of the net profit in 1950 than in 1949 ( 50*8 per cent vs. 51-6 per cent).
(4)	There was a wide variation in results both as between groups and between individual companies within the groups.
(7)	The net working capital position of the 362 firms was strengthened by 18-3 per cent in 1950, with every group showing an improvement.
(8)	The combined net asset position of the 362 firms was increased by 9-1 per cent with all groups showing a higher net worth.
The article goes on to indicate that there was a great improvement in the percentage of profits and of business activity in 1950 over 1949, and that the prospects for this year are even better. That is our point, Mr. Speaker. We maintain that we can obtain a greater percentage of our revenue from some of these corporations, particularly the larger ones, than provision is made for in this bill. Something is happening at the present time that is quite unusual in Canadian business history, at least unusual until recent years. These unusual profits are being invested in real wealth, in plant, equipment, land, real estate, and assets of that sort. The
Income Tax Act
large corporations of this country are investing their excess profits in a form of wealth that will be largely unaffected by future inflation. They are placing themselves in a very strong position with respect to the increasing inflationary period that may come in the future, while at the same time the general public is asked to curtail expenditure, particularly consumer expenditure, and, as a result of these savings in the purchasing of consumer goods, to invest either by savings in the bank or by the purchase of bonds.
We believe, Mr. Speaker, that this process is wrong at the present time; and that it is adding to inflation. We believe that these companies should be seeking new capital investment, and that the state should be getting a larger percentage of these excess profits in order to reduce inflation and decrease the burden on the lower income groups.
This great expansion out of profits in Canada at the present time in a form of wealth which will be largely unaffected by any future inflation is being carried on at the expense generally of the Canadian public. The result of that type of expansion, Mr. Speaker, is that more and more wealth is getting into fewer and fewer hands. If companies were required to carry on their expansion as a result of raising new capital the wealth would at least to some extent be more diversified and in a greater number of hands.
As against that, the worker is asked to save, and his savings are largely in the form of bank savings or in small bonds. He is being asked to save in a form that will be seriously affected by any inflation that occurs in the future.
What is the position of the low income groups at the present time? The people I am speaking of now particularly are married people on incomes of $3,000 or less, and single people on incomes of $1,500 or less. The cost of living is going up monthly. Nobody can deny that. The cost of food, the cost of clothing, the cost of shelter, the cost of living and the cost of the necessities of life to keep the human organism alive and working are going up all the time. In addition to that the cost of housing is going up. That is a very important matter so far as this lower income group is concerned, because it is within this group that we find the greatest need for housing in Canada at the present time. I hold in my hand a clipping from the Financial Post of May 26 which reads:
British Columbia
Building costs:	Vancouver building costs have
climbed about 25 per cent in the past year and are still moving upward. A survey by a New York firm of consulting engineers places the index at 171-2

Income Tax Act
in March, 1950, and at 203-8 In March of this year. Calculated on ordinary frame houses, the index takes into consideration costs of lumber, plumbing, wages and1 other key materials and services.
Before passing on I want to make a point. The cost of housing has gone up 25 per cent in Vancouver. People are often inclined to say that wages have gone up and have increased the cost of building. They have to some extent, but wages have not increased 25 per cent in Vancouver in the building trade in the last twelve months; this increase represents profits. This means that as against the position of the large corporations with excess profits to invest in the expansion of capital, plant and equipment, we have these groups with no reserves, with a greater difficulty to live from day to day, facing an insecure future, with this tax actually to some extent increasing their cost of living and no opportunity for expansion in any direction whatever.
In conclusion, what is the position from our point of view? Against what background do we in this group believe we should plan this income Tax Act at this time on a fairer basis? Here we have the corporations with expanding profits, and the low income groups that I have mentioned with a lowering standard of living, to be further lowered by increased taxation. With democracy demanding equality of sacrifice, surely at a time like this when Canada is facing a very serious defence problem we should do all we can in the house to promote at least to some extent equality of sacrifice, so far as taxation is concerned. Therefore I move, seconded by the hon. member for Saskatoon (Mr. Knight):
That this bill be not now read a second time but that it be resolved that in the opinion of this house consideration should be given by the government to altering the provisions with respect to corporation income tax so as to levy graduated taxation on excess profits.
In conclusion I urge hon. members, when they consider voting on this amendment, which we are very much concerned about, to consider carefully those Canadians who are losing their lives in Korea, Canadians who are being wounded and other Canadians who are having great difficulty at this time to carry on because of the increased cost of living. I am sure if hon. members give consideration to those facts, and face this question fairly, they will realize they will be fully justified in supporting the amendment as an attempt to introduce to some extent into this taxation a measure of equality of sacrifice.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Although this has nothing to do with this particular clause, I want to confirm an understanding, which was arrived at when we were in committee, that by unanimous consent it will be in order to discuss depreciation.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to raise a question with respect to income tax which is based upon an exemplary case which must have been repeated many times throughout Canada and which no doubt has come to the attention of the minister on previous occasions. I refer to a single lady who has looked1 after a maiden aunt who was aged and destitute and who would have been homeless if her devoted niece had not provided for her during the year. This single person maintained a home in which she kept her aunt and was able to claim relief under the Income Tax Act because she was maintaining a home in which she supported herself. In other words, she came under that section which provides:
... a person wholly dependent upon him and connected with him by blood relationship, marriage or adoption . . .
In 1950 this single lady married. She still has a taxable income and still looks after her aged infirm maiden aunt. However, her claim for an allowance for a dependent has been disallowed. I understand that she could claim for a parent, a grandparent, a brother, a sister, a daughter or a sister training as a nurse, a brother-in-law, a sister-in-law or a child who is not legally adopted. It seems strange that these other claims can be made but a case which apparently is such a strong one must of course be ruled out under the present regulations and the law. Would the minister give some indication whether or not the government can adapt their policy so as to take care of what looks like a very worthy case such as the one I have just described?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I will consider very carefully the facts which my hon. friend has presented. I did not want to interrupt him, but this
Income Tax Act
question of exemptions for other than specified dependents in the act is a very broad one. I do not think it is strictly relevant to discuss it under this section. As I pointed out, it was arranged that we were going to discuss the subject of depreciation. However, I will consider the facts that he has put forward, and perhaps at an appropriate time before we finish consideration of the bill I will try to give him a considered answer on it.

I should like to make a few brief observations on the question of depreciation which I think has an importance very great and perhaps different from what some of us thought at the time that it was originally brought forward by the minister. I will read briefly from what the minister said in his budget speech at page 1808 of Hansard. After speaking about the tremendous investment program facing us in the year ahead the minister said:
What we need is a stiff financial deterrent that will affect particularly the businessman who is considering the kind of investment which is attractive, not because of its long-term soundness, but because it can be written off out of the expected high profits of the next few years at a time when he expects the rate of corporate income tax to be abnormally high.
Then the minister refers in a general way to the nature of the deterrent, and I want to read something that he said later because I think it is very important to have in mind that this is the type of thing the minister was picturing to us. I want to suggest that what this provision may do is to have results that are far enough off from the minister's intention unless it is very broadly interpreted, and indeed I think unless some changes are made in the regulations. The minister went on to say:
The deterrent will particularly affect the businessman whose decision to make a capital expenditure is strongly influenced by the expectation that he can write off a large fraction of his cost ... In other words it will compel the businessman to give primary attention to the long-term prospects of proposed capital expenditures and if outside financial participation is required lenders will also take this view.
What I want to draw attention to at the outset is that the whole tenor of this is that it is to affect big business, people who are wanting to go into business in a big way-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: My hon. friend is wrong about that. It is to affect everyone, big and small.

I say the
atmosphere that the minister created is rather of the big man. It is because it does affect the big man-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
That was completely unintentional, if that is the case.

Income Tax Act

At any rate I am coming to the other aspect of it because what I want to ask him to consider particularly is that it affects the small as well as the big. It is that point I wish to emphasize particularly. I do not agree by any means with all that the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Herridge) said a little while ago, but I agree very heartily with the fear he expressed that in the circumstances in which we find ourselves at the moment, and with the development of the defence economy, we may find it harder and harder for small men to originate small businesses or, as he put it, we may find more and more wealth passing into fewer and fewer hands. That is something that should not be disregarded.
I want to refer in passing to the regulations which will come up again. I point out also in passing that the purpose is really twofold. First of all it is to act as a bit of a damper on expansion, and second I presume it is to conserve necessary defence materials. That may be ancillary, but I think it is not irrelevant. I want to point out next that there is the greatest danger as the matter stands that it will be almost impossible for new businesses to start up, and I even suggest to the minister that it should be considered whether there may not be an exemption of businesses of a certain size. I am not prepared to dogmatize as to the amount, but I suggest very earnestly that we should try not to allow this to create a situation which will make it difficult, if not impossible, for new businesses to arise, because we are not considering something which is going to last for a month or a year. As now contemplated it will last for four years, and if we create a situation for four years which is going to make it, as I say, difficult if not impossible for small businesses to arise, or at any rate make it very much harder for them, I think that is a very serious thing and should be so considered.
I next want to bring to the attention of the minister certain specific types of cases which it seems to me will arise, and the problems of which I hope can be most seriously considered. I am not overlooking the fact that there is a wide range of exceptions, and that beyond the exception there is a discretion. I am not overlooking that at all, but having said that I wish to bring certain cases to attention which I think are pertinent, and in some cases urgent. I hope they will be considered on their merits, and that we may have an answer with regard to each of them.
First of all I wish to go back and read one operative clause from what the minister said in his budget speech. At page 1808 of Hansard he said:
To provide this deterrent it is proposed to defer for a period of four years the right to charge depreciation on all capital assets acquired after April 10, 1951, excepting certain classes of assets defined in the regulations and certain additional kinds of assets when certified as eligible by the Minister of Trade and Commerce.
The types of cases I wish to bring up are these. The first is where a business was committed, at the time the order became effective, to capital expenditure. In other words, it was not a case of making a decision after the minister's speech, after the coming into effect. There was a capital investment commitment made before that. Second, there is the case of businesses which merely change the form of ownership after the order becomes effective. For example you have a single business which is turned into a corporation, or a partnership turned into a limited liability company, or the case of a man dying, leaving his business to his son and creating a situation where the business has to be sold. If the right to depreciation is gone in such a case we shall have a serious lessening of the value of the property. Finally I want to reiterate again what I said, that I hope special consideration will be given to the position of those wishing to start up small businesses, and on these points I should like to hear the minister's comments.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
On the points that have been raised by my hon. friend, first I should say that the regulations are being reviewed at the moment. I understand that the Minister of National Revenue, with the concurrence of myself and the Minister of Trade and Commerce, very shortly will be recommending certain amendments to these regulations in the light of the experience we have had in the three or four weeks since the original regulations were put in, in the light of applications which have been made, and so on. Among other things I might say that provision will be made under which the names of those given certificates of eligibility, together with the reasons for which they were given, will be published, probably in the official gazette. In any case that will be provided in the regulations.
Consideration is being given to the problem raised by my hon. friend of a change in the form of ownership, and I think probably the Minister of Trade and Commerce, the Minister of National Revenue and myself will be making some announcement about

that before very long. On the question of small businesses, it is pretty hard to say what a small business is. As my hon. friend knows, the rate of corporation income tax on the smaller businesses is very much lower than on the large businesses. It was 10 per cent; it is now 15 per cent. I do not think any serious hardship would be suffered by these smaller businesses if depreciation were postponed on the assets they may acquire.
I want to make it clear that this measure is not aimed at large businesses as such or at small businesses as such, but at all businesses. The main purpose of the proposal is to cause businessmen to defer less essential expenditures, and to be perfectly satisfied that the asset they are acquiring is one they are willing to keep for a number of years and which will be profitable for a number of years, so that on the expiration of the period during which depreciation is deferred they will still be in a position to make profits against which the capital cost allowances can be taken.

I appreciate what the minister has said, but I would like to ask one or two things. The minister has indicated that changes are in contemplation. May I take it that when these changes are made an opportunity will be provided in the near future to discuss the matter again in the house?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I cannot give any positive
assurance as to that in the light of the probable sessional program. My hon. friend appreciates that these regulations are made under section 11 of the Income Tax Act, which provides for capital cost allowances. The granting of capital cost allowances is made by regulation, on the recommendation of the Minister of National Revenue. In strict theory he does not have to do so; but of course, as I explained, this is a matter for determination by regulation. Under the old act it was purely a matter of ministerial discretion; under the new act it is provided by regulation. I should hope that the regulations would be completed and perhaps tabled before the estimates of the Department of National Revenue are finished. Unquestionably at that time there would be an opportunity to question the minister about them, though I think perhaps a more satisfactory course would be to have that discussion when the estimates of the Minister of Trade and Commerce were under consideration, because it is by his department that the certificates of eligibility are being issued. The Department of National Revenue will have the responsibility of determining questions of fact such as when particular assets were acquired, and so on. I cannot
Income Tax Act
give a positive assurance that the amendments, which I hope will be available within a few days, will be discussed, but I should think there would be that opportunity and certainly I would do what I could to provide a suitable time at which that discussion could take place.

Purely as
a matter of what seems a convenient practice, with these changes likely to be available in a few days, I take it that submissions could be made to the proper authority continuing this discussion, in the hope that some of the things we bring up now may be felt worthy of consideration. These regulations are not like the laws of the Medes and Persians.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Oh, no.

I take it
they are flexible; that is the reason they are left in regulation form, is it not?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is it exactly. This is a new move. The government wants to make the regulations as reasonable as possible, to cause as little dislocation as possible and yet achieve the objective in view. The department is always ready to listen, and in fact welcomes representations from businessmen and others who may be affected, in order to ensure that the regulations are drawn as well as possible.

That seems a very sensible way to deal with the situation. While I am on my feet I might as well mention one or two other points so they will be on record and those who are considering the regulations will have them before them. Another question that arises is the depreciation of used equipment and buildings which pass into the hands of new owners. Obviously there is a situation there. Then there is the question of the depreciation where the capital asset acquired has been used by a former owner, though some kind of safeguard would be necessary so it would be clear that the transaction was genuine. Probably it should be in the hands of the former owner for a period of twelve months, say. Finally there is the case where you have a business property on which the purchaser had an option to purchase dated prior to April 10. I am not going to delay the committee by dwelling further on these points. I am glad to know the regulations are flexible, and that these matters can be brought up and discussed further from time to time.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

speechtext: I would like the minister to explain this deferred depreciation a little more clearly, because I have heard two or three versions. I imagine the correct one is that if you buy a new piece of machinery you lose four years' depreciation. Some people seem to think that when 1956 comes around they will get the four years' depreciation all at once, but I do not think that is right. Would the minister explain it?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: To put it shortly, this is pushing the whole period forward. Suppose an article was acquired in June of 1951. If this rule were not in force depreciation would commence in 1951. Instead of that the right to take depreciation or capital cost allowance is deferred for four years. After that four-year period the owner can take the depreciation he could have taken in 1951. In 1955, let us say, he can take the depreciation he could have taken now, in 1956 the depreciation he could have taken in 1952, and so oh until the asset is fully depreciated. I want to emphasize that the right to depreciation is simply postponed; it is not taken away. So long as earnings are available after the expiration of the period, then the depreciation can be taken.

As I said during the budget debate, I think this is a very foolish change for the minister to make. I have a very high regard for him, but I believe he has made a mistake in this case. For many years the depreciation rate was 10 per cent, and everyone knew exactly what to expect and just what to do. Even in times of great crisis, even when our profits' tax had to go to seventy-five per cent, or say it did, as long as you had a steady rate of depreciation and knew what you were doing, business could keep on going along on a sound basis. But now, when you get fooling around with depreciation, and fooling around with everything, you get to a point where nobody knows what he is doing. I believe the minister was ill advised to change these rates of depreciation. He should have left it the way it was.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I suppose we have been discussing depreciation, Mr. Chairman, but the clause itself does not relate to that.

Mr. Chairman, the minister has given some indication to the house that the present order in council, which I believe is P.C. 1778 dated April 10, is now under review, and that certain amendments may be made to that order. I believe that that fact probably makes it all the more desirable,

since the minister has not indicated the nature of the probable amendment-perhaps he is not in a position to do so-that any views hon. members may have concerning this measure should be put forward at this point, in the hope that they may receive consideration when the amendments to the order in council are being determined.
There are one or two aspects of the view put forward by the minister in regard to this whole subject that I believe deserve comment. The minister has stated that one of the objectives of the proposals to defer depreciation is to encourage business enterprises, where possible, to defer physical expansion of their plant and equipment. Now, I suppose every one of us will say that, so far as that will make a contribution towards conserving essential defence materials that may be in short supply, the purpose is worthy of support. Again, to the extent to which this measure may be intended to reduce postpone-able expenditures, and to increase savings, about which we were speaking earlier in the evening, I think the house would wish to approach the proposals favourably. On the other hand, Mr. Chairman, we have to assess the professed purpose that the minister has assigned in relation to the facts as we see them developing since April 10.
I am glad the minister has spoken as he has tonight in clarifying the issue, because unquestionably the words he used on pages 1808 and 1809 of Hansard of April 10, have carried the impression abroad that his policy was directed against new and smaller businesses. The minister tonight has sought to correct that impression, and to stress that it is of general application. Nevertheless, Mr. Chairman, the fact of the matter is that the weight of this new policy is going to be felt particularly by newer businesses, younger businesses and businesses which are in the course of expansion. They are going to be now compelled either to arrest their expansion or forgo what is a very important element in their financial plans, namely, depreciation. So we may say that a young or growing industry is the one that will feel the effects of this new policy most severely at the present time.
To that extent, any measure of this kind is necessarily discriminatory. This is not going to hurt any business that had the good fortune to carry out any needed expansion of physical facilities or physical plant prior to April 10. It is a matter of luck that some industries acquired their physical plant or assets prior to April 10, and will be permitted to depreciate them in the ordinary way, while other businesses, in the midst of expansion and the

growing pains of a young business, but which did not acquire the physical plant prior to April 10, are now going to feel the full weight of this new policy. This is a regrettable form of discrimination. It may be inevitable in measures of this kind.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It is true of steel control, too.

I say, it may be inevitable in any measure of this kind, but nevertheless the effect of it is discriminatory.
The hon. member for Greenwood raised the problem of the application of this new policy in circumstances in which it is, in effect, given a retroactive operation. The test which is laid down by the minister, and which found its way into order in council P.C. 1778, is acquisition of the particular assets by the taxpayer up to April 10. Now, sir, that word, itself, as a test presents no little difficulty. I am hopeful that the minister, having had the problem brought before him tonight by the member for Greenwood, is going to endeavour to do something to soften the severity of order in council P.C. 1778 with respect to those taxpayers who had entered into commitments up to April 10, but who had not then acquired the particular physical assets which would otherwise have been subject to depreciation.
Sir, there are not a few cases of that kind, where in the ordinary course the particular taxpayer has made a binding commitment prior to April 10, a commitment which had not been carried to the point where delivery of the physical asset had been made to him prior to that date, but where he is compelled by the nature of his commitment to proceed and to purchase the particular asset which would otherwise be depreciable for tax purposes. I am sure there must have been many
Income Tax Act
cases of that type brought to the attention of the minister. I expect most hon. members in this committee have had some such cases brought to their personal attention. Now, those are cases of real hardship because had those particular taxpayers been aware in time, it is certain that in a great many cases they would not have entered into the commitment to acquire assets of the type upon which they are not now to be entitled to any depreciation allowance.
Section stands.
Progress reported.
